entities.name: Banco Ambrosiano
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Banco Ambrosiano was an Italian bank founded in 1896 in Milan as a Catholic banking institution, which collapsed in 1982 in Italy's greatest financial scandal of the 20th century, involving the Vatican Bank (IOR), Freemasonry (Lodge P2), and the Mafia in one of history's most extraordinary corruption cases. The bank's chairman Roberto Calvi was found hanging from Blackfriars Bridge in London in June 1982 — initially ruled suicide but later ruled murder — earning him the nickname 'God's Banker' due to his Vatican connections.

Banco Ambrosiano's collapse involved a complex web of offshore shell companies in Panama and the Bahamas, through which approximately $1.3 billion had been siphoned, leaving unpaid creditors. The Vatican Bank (IOR) had guaranteed many Ambrosiano loans and was found to be heavily implicated, ultimately paying $250 million to creditors as a 'voluntary contribution' without admitting legal liability.

The P2 Masonic lodge scandal connected Ambrosiano to Licio Gelli's network that included senior Italian military officers, politicians, journalists, and judges — essentially a secret government within the state. Calvi's murder (eventually attributed to Mafia figures by Italian courts) and the subsequent Vatican Bank reforms mark the Ambrosiano affair as the Vatican's most damaging financial scandal. Pope John Paul II acknowledged the affair's seriousness; subsequent Vatican Bank reforms were prompted partly by the Ambrosiano scandal.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Banco Ambrosiano scandal — linking the Vatican Bank, Freemasonry, the Mafia, and a mysterious murder under London's Blackfriars Bridge — is Italy's most sensational financial crime and prompted Vatican financial reforms that continue to this day.
